| [LIT-1681](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1681.md) | A Perfect Moral Storm: Climate Change, Intergenerational Ethics and the Problem of Moral Corruption | Gardiner (2006). Climate change is a "perfect moral storm": three problems that threaten ethical action converge in it. The global storm is the familiar reading, a tragedy of the commons between states with no effective global governance, worsened by uncertainty about national impacts, a status quo bias and skewed vulnerabilities. The intergenerational storm is worse. Carbon dioxide's long life makes climate change resilient, backloaded and deferred, so the benefits of emitting fall to the present and the costs to later generations. That is a Pure Intergenerational Problem, in which every generation rationally overpollutes and the usual remedies are unavailable, because the generations do not coexist. The theoretical storm is that our theories handle uncertainty, intergenerational equity and contingent persons badly. Together they invite moral corruption: by selective attention, each generation can seem to act while exploiting its position in time, and need not admit it, even to itself. Even the prominence of the global model may be such a convenience, since it assumes states represent their citizens "in perpetuity". | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md)) from the publisher's PDF, republished with White Horse Press's permission on the Rachel Carson Center's Environment & Society Portal (environmentandsociety.org/node/5976); worth reading as the short statement of why concern for future generations fails in practice: a self-interest that is generation-relative, and a moral motive that can be corrupted without being given up. |
| [LIT-1684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1684.md) | The Case for Strong Longtermism | Greaves & MacAskill. Argue for axiological and deontic strong longtermism: in the most important decisions facing agents today (how a society or an individual spends resources without restriction to a cause, and career choice), every near-best option is near-best for the far future and delivers much larger benefits there than in the near future, and one ought to choose such an option. The argument rests on an expected number of future beings of at least 10^24 (10^14 on a restricted, Earth-only estimate), and on interventions (asteroid detection, pandemic preparedness, AI safety) whose expected far-future benefit per $100 beats the 0.025 lives that bednets save. The deontic thesis follows by a stakes-sensitivity argument that any plausible non-consequentialism should accept. The authors take cluelessness, ambiguity aversion and imprecise credences to fail as objections. They name fanaticism about tiny probabilities as one of the most plausible ways the case could fail. They concede that a positive pure rate of time preference would defeat it. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1302](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1302.md)) from the authors' working paper (GPI Working Paper No. 5-2021, June 2021) on the Global Priorities Institute's site, an earlier version of the 2025 chapter; worth reading as the precise statement of strong longtermism and of exactly which assumptions it needs (zero pure time preference, expected value at small probabilities); it says nothing about why anyone would act on it. |
| [LIT-1688](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1688.md) | High Risk, Low Reward: A Challenge to the Astronomical Value of Existential Risk Mitigation | Thorstad (2023). Argues, inside expected-value reasoning and with no special ethical premises, that pessimism about existential risk weakens the case for mitigating it. On Ord's simple model, cutting this century's risk by a fraction is worth that fraction of one century, whatever the risk; with absolute cuts, value growth or cuts in every century, higher risk makes mitigation worth less. Astronomical value returns only on a "time of perils" hypothesis in which risk falls soon and stays very low, and he argues that appeals to growing wisdom, an existential risk Kuznets curve and space settlement do not support it. Mitigation may still be valuable, "but perhaps not astronomically so". | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1308](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1308.md)) from the author's penultimate draft (GPI Working Paper No. 6-2023, July 2023) on the Global Priorities Institute's site; worth reading as a demonstration, inside the longtermist's own expected-value framework, that high existential risk lowers the value of reducing it unless risk soon falls and stays low. |
| [LIT-1691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1691.md) | Generativity as a Route to Active Ageing | A gerontological essay with a report of the authors' own studies. It reads Erikson's generativity, as McAdams models it, as the psychological form of an ethical category of "joint responsibility", and argues it is a lifelong concern, not a midlife task. It restates McAdams' model: generativity springs from cultural demand and from an inner desire made of a "need to be needed" and a need for symbolic immortality, and passes through concern, commitment and belief in the species to action and a life-story script. It distinguishes generativity from altruism and says generative engagement can be selfish or altruistic in motive. Studies of 3,308 people aged 59 to 108 in Mexico, Spain and Germany found generativity predicted optimism and life satisfaction beyond health, money and family status. An intervention of intergenerational dialogue projects in Belarus, Russia and Ukraine raised Loyola Generativity Scale scores in old and young participants. No test statistics are reported. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1261](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1261.md)), in place of [LIT-1777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1777.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a compact restatement of McAdams' model of generativity, with symbolic immortality as one of its motives, and for its claim that generativity serves the well-being of the old. |
| [LIT-1712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1712.md) | Why Worry About Future Generations? | Scheffler (2018), the Uehiro Lectures. Argues that our reasons to care about future generations are not only reasons of beneficence toward their welfare: they also come from our valuing, our attachments to people, practices and traditions, and our stake in the human story's going on, so that caring about the future is partly a matter of caring about what we value now. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher, and NYU's repository lists it without a file. Scheffler's 2015 Uehiro Lectures, which presented draft material for the book, are open as audio at Oxford's Practical Ethics site (practicalethics.ox.ac.uk/node/2950046); they were not transcribed, so no work was read in its place. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). |
| [LIT-1739](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1739.md) | Astronomical Waste: The Opportunity Cost of Delayed Technological Development | Bostrom (2003). On an aggregative, undiscounted view, each second's delay in settling the Virgo Supercluster loses the potential for about 10^29 human lives if minds can run on computers, or 10^13 if they must be biological. Yet the same arithmetic makes safety, not speed, the total utilitarian's priority: a one-percentage-point cut in existential risk is worth a delay of over 10 million years, so "Maximize expected aggregate utility!" becomes "Minimize existential risk!". On a person-affecting view, which counts only people who exist or will exist, extinction is bad for what it does to people now alive. Then, given a non-negligible chance that some of them live to share the cosmic benefits through life extension, existential safety is very important but must be balanced against speed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1314](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1314.md)) from the text on Bostrom's own site; worth reading as the original form of the argument from the size of the possible future, and for its statement of how a person-affecting view changes it: toward the interests of people now alive. |
| [LIT-1740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1740.md) | The Misfortunes of the Dead | Pitcher (1984). Distinguishes the ante-mortem person, who lived, from the post-mortem person, who is dead, and argues that the dead can be wronged and harmed: an event after death, such as slander or a broken promise, makes it true that the ante-mortem person was harmed, without backward causation. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; the 1984 article is closed at JSTOR and the 1993 reprint at De Gruyter. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Luper's SEP entry on death ([LIT-1792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1792.md)). |
| [LIT-1747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1747.md) | What We Owe the Future | MacAskill (2022). The book-length case for longtermism for a general audience: future people count, there may be vastly many of them, and we can affect how their lives go, by influencing which values become entrenched and by reducing the risks of extinction, collapse and stagnation. It defends the view that a larger population of good lives is better. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; the book's own site posts its endnotes and supplementary materials, not its chapters. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: MacAskill, Thomas and Vallinder's SPC framework (LIT-1778). |
| [LIT-1753](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1753.md) | The epistemic challenge to longtermism | Tarsney (2023). The epistemic challenge to longtermism: our ability to predictably affect the future may fade fast enough that far-future effects do not dominate. He models a $1 million longtermist intervention (existential risk reduction) whose effect lasts until an "exogenous nullifying event", arriving at a constant rate r, and compares it with a global-health benchmark. With deliberately conservative inputs, longtermism wins only if r is below about 0.000135 per year when humanity settles the stars, or about 0.000000012 per year when it stays on Earth. Mixing in small credences in space settlement, a low r, fast settlement or very efficient conversion of stars into value makes longtermism win by orders of magnitude. But on some plausible views that win rests on minuscule probabilities of astronomical payoffs, so the case depends either on non-obvious empirical claims or on tolerating Pascalian fanaticism. Even where longtermism wins, most of its expected value may fall within thousands or millions of years. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1247](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1247.md)) from the author's working paper (GPI Working Paper No. 3-2022, version 4, April 2022) on the Global Priorities Institute's site; worth reading as the most careful quantitative statement of the epistemic objection to longtermism, and as a demonstration that the expected-value reply to it comes to rest on very small probabilities. |
| [LIT-1754](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1754.md) | Death and the Afterlife | Scheffler (2013), his 2012 Tanner Lectures with replies. The afterlife conjecture: much of what we value depends on our confidence that humanity will go on after our deaths (a "collective afterlife"), as the doomsday and infertility scenarios show, so we care about people who will live after us, whom we will never know. He also argues that personal immortality would drain value of its point. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. Open Library lists the book for print-disabled readers only. Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures, the book's first two chapters, are open at tannerlectures.org. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures ([LIT-1779](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1779.md)) and Cottingham's NDPR review ([LIT-1784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1784.md)). |
| [LIT-1756](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1756.md) | Intergenerational Justice | Meyer (2003; revised 2026). The SEP entry on what present people owe future and past people, which argues a position as well as surveying. Future people's contingency on our choices, the non-identity problem, defeats harm understood as making someone worse off than before or than otherwise. It does not defeat a threshold notion of harm, on which we harm a person by causing her to exist, or to be, below a normatively set threshold. Combined with the counterfactual notion, this gives a "disjunctive" harm. The threshold is best read as sufficientarian, in basic needs or capabilities, rather than egalitarian or prioritarian; Rawls's just savings principle is one version. The entry is weakly person-affecting, so it owes merely possible people nothing, and it grants that this gives no reason to prefer a flourishing future to none. That gap is filled by concerns that are not rights: Scheffler's afterlife conjecture, and an obligation owed to present and past people not to destroy the goods and practices on which future-oriented projects depend. Historical injustice is treated with the same notions of harm. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1304](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1304.md)) from the SEP entry, substantive revision of 17 July 2026, with its notes; worth reading as the standard map of the person-affecting side of the obligations question, by an author who argues for a threshold, sufficientarian reading of it and says where rights run out. |
| [LIT-1761](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1761.md) v2 | Shaping Humanity's Longterm Trajectory | Ord (2025). A framework for comparing ways present action could change humanity's long-run future. Humanity's "instantaneous value" over time is a curve; the future's value is the area under it, and an intervention's value is the area between the default and the altered curve. Value must be roughly quantitative and separable across time, with no pure time preference. Four idealised changes have values that do not depend on the curve's shape: an advancement (the future reached δt sooner) is worth about (v_τ − v_0)δt, independent of the future's duration τ, and about −v_0δt if the end comes sooner too; a speed-up scales with (v_τ − v̄)τ; a gain (a fixed rise in value) with τ; an enhancement (a proportional rise) with v̄τ. Raising the chance of surviving near-term existential risk by a factor γ_p is worth (γ_p − 1)v̄τ, like an enhancement, and meets the bar of contingency more easily. So it is hard for advancing progress to rival existential risk reduction: on a million-year future, a year's advancement is worth about a one-in-a-million gain in survival chance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1269.md)), in place of [LIT-1678](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1678.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as Ord's own formal statement of why reducing existential risk dominates other ways of shaping the future, and of the evaluative assumptions (time-separable value, no pure time preference) that this needs. |
| [LIT-1763](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1763.md) | Population and Having Children Now | Narveson (2017). Returns to his 1967 and 1973 theme, that utilitarianism commits one to making people happy and not to making happy people, after abandoning utilitarianism. He holds that creating a person neither benefits nor harms them: before conception there is no one to confer life on, and without a prior person harm and benefit lack a comparator. Yet, "contrary, perhaps" to how he was read, the existence of people with good lives is normally a good thing and a reason to create them. It matters to us because parents and the benevolent like it, and because more people benefit those around them. Morality's enforceable part, though, licenses interfering with procreation only when it would harm actual persons, "alive, breathing, and acting now (or at any rate in their lifetimes)", never for possible ones. Not helping the poor instead of having a child is not harming them. Against Benatar, a life's goods can outweigh its harms. The second half argues, with little evidence, that resources are created rather than fixed, that current climate policy is inefficient, and that no general conflict between present and future people exists. Parents may have as many children as they want and can afford. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1318](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1318.md)), in place of [LIT-1769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1769.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the founder of the person-affecting slogan restating it late: creating happy people is good but owed to no one, and only harm to actual people can bind; read in place of the 1973 paper ([LIT-1769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1769.md)), which it summarizes in one sentence. Its second half is a polemic on resources and climate, not argument. |
| [LIT-1768](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1768.md) | Future People, the Non-Identity Problem, and Person-Affecting Principles | Parfit (2017), his last paper, submitted unfinished the day before his death. Most of our choices of policy change who will exist, so a policy that makes later lives much worse may be worse for no one who ever lives: the non-identity problem. Narrow person-affecting principles, on which nothing can be worse, or wrong, if it is worse for no one, then imply that such policies, and even ending human history by all choosing childlessness, are not wrong. Parfit rejects them, and rejects solutions that appeal to rights, wronging or Boonin's acceptance of the implausible conclusions. He also retracts his own earlier appeal to an impersonal principle. Instead, being caused to exist with a life worth living is an intrinsic, existential benefit, and on a Wide Person-Affecting Principle one outcome is worse if it benefits people less. That solves the non-identity problem in person-affecting terms and keeps "better than" transitive, where the Weak Narrow Principle and the Two-Tier View do not. For different numbers he proposes a Wide Dual Principle, counting both the benefits to each and the benefits to all. It does not imply the Repugnant Conclusion, though Parfit grants that this alone does not let us avoid it. He allows that we may be permitted, or required, to favour present people over greater benefits to future people, but warns that done by every generation this could "wreck the Earth". | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md)) from the publisher's PDF as reprinted in The Philosophers' Annual vol. 37 (philosophersannual.org); worth reading as Parfit's final answer to his own non-identity problem, which puts obligations to future people on a person-affecting footing without making them owed to anyone in particular. |
| [LIT-1769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1769.md) | Moral Problems of Population | Narveson (1973). Argues that utilitarian concern is for the welfare of people who exist or will exist, so it gives reason to make people happy but none to bring happy people into existence: the founding statement of the person-affecting view in population ethics. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. Oxford Academic and PhilArchive answered with Cloudflare challenges, and PhilArchive's record lists no file. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Narveson 2017 (LIT-1763). |
| [LIT-1773](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1773.md) | Existential Risk Prevention as Global Priority | Bostrom (2013). Defines existential risk as a threat of premature extinction of Earth-originating intelligent life or of the permanent and drastic destruction of its potential for desirable development: risks of at least crushing severity and pan-generational scope. Gives four classes (human extinction, permanent stagnation, flawed realisation, subsequent ruination), the last two defined normatively. On an aggregative, time-neutral view even Earth alone could hold 10^16 future lives, so cutting the risk by a millionth of a percentage point is worth a hundred million lives. Hence the maxipok rule of thumb for impersonal moral action: maximise the probability of an outcome that avoids existential catastrophe. Other ethical views (Adams' shared project of humanity, preference satisfaction, custodial duties to ancestors and descendants) concur to differing degrees. Under moral uncertainty, keeping options open recasts sustainability as a trajectory. The risk is neglected: in Scopus, papers on "human extinction" number fewer than those on dung beetles. It is also undersupplied, as a pan-generational public good that even a world state could only partly capture. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md)) from the published version posted on Bostrom's existential-risk site; worth reading as the standard definition and typology of existential risk, and for the record's purposes as the one longtermist source that discusses motivation: it diagnoses a "deficit of motivation" and gives, through Adams, a ground in humanity's shared project. |
| [LIT-1778](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1778.md) | The Significance, Persistence, Contingency Framework | MacAskill, Thomas & Vallinder (2022). A short technical note that formalises the heuristic of *What We Owe the Future*, chapter 2. The value an originating event E contributes through a feature F of the world factors exactly as significance (ΔV/ΔT, value per unit of the extra time), persistence (T, how long F lasts) and contingency (ΔT/T, the share of F's duration due to E), with marginal and expected-value forms in which the factors are ex ante quantities, not expectations of the factors. An alternative makes significance independent of the counterfactual (V/T) and contingency the sum of the semi-elasticities of significance, persistence and the probability that F is present. The SPC estimate feeds the "importance" factor of the importance–tractability–neglectedness framework, and the note proposes reading tractability as overall easiness times "leverage". It assumes expected-value maximisation and makes no ethical argument. status_note: worth reading as the formal statement of how *What We Owe the Future* values an act's effect on the long-run future, read in place of the book; it gives the book's accounting, not its argument that future people count. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1300](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1300.md)), in place of [LIT-1747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1747.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the formal statement of how *What We Owe the Future* values an act's effect on the long-run future, read in place of the book; it gives the book's accounting, not its argument that future people count. |
| [LIT-1784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1784.md) | Review of Samuel Scheffler, Death and the Afterlife | A short NDPR review of Scheffler's *Death and the Afterlife*. It summarizes the afterlife conjecture and the conclusion that "our own survival is less important to us than the survival of the human race" in one specific sense. It reports the third lecture: life must be temporally bounded, so personal immortality is no remedy, yet confidence in our values depends on others living on. It reports Frankfurt's Darwinian doubt that the concern is altruistic, and Wolf's argument that people facing extinction could and should "snap out of it". It faults all parties for ignoring religious thought on finitude. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1306](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1306.md)), in place of [LIT-1754](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1754.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the only account the record holds of the book's third lecture and of Wolf's and Frankfurt's commentaries; read its "more altruistic construal" against Scheffler's own denial of altruism. |
| [LIT-1792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1792.md) | Death | The SEP survey of the philosophy of death, revised in 2026. Luper gives a compositional account of life (an object is alive when its parts control what composes it, under information they carry) and defines death as the loss of the capacity for vital activities. He reconstructs Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us. He shows that it fails if welfare is not only pleasure or if things can harm by precluding goods: the deprivationist defense. He surveys answers to when death harms (concurrentism, priorism, subsequentism, indefinitism, atemporalism), Lucretius's symmetry argument, and posthumous harm, where Pitcher's desire-based account locates the harm in the living person. He sides with Williams's critics: immortality need not be tedious. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1294.md)), in place of [LIT-1740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1740.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a map of the death-harm debate with its premises made explicit. It gives Pitcher's account of posthumous harm in a paragraph, without his ante-mortem person. |
| [LIT-1852](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1852.md) | The Nature of Epistemic Injustice | Maitra (2010), Philosophical Books 51(4), a critical study of Fricker's Epistemic Injustice. It reports the book's definitions with its pages: testimonial injustice is a credibility deficit owed to the hearer's identity prejudice (pp. 19, 28, 35), and hermeneutical injustice is having a significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding by hermeneutical marginalization, systematic or incidental (pp. 153, 155, 158). It argues the testimonial account is too broad, since a hearer owes a speaker a matched credibility judgement only in some relationships, and too narrow, since epistemic bad luck and stereotypes held through careless evidence-gathering can also wrong a speaker; and that both kinds of injustice mix individual and structural prejudice. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1428](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1428.md)) in full, from the author's draft of 14 July 2010 on her University of Michigan page (https://public.websites.umich.edu/~imaitra/Research/NEI0710.pdf), which the owner ruled a lawful copy on 2026-10-30. The draft is marked "Draft – Please do not cite without author's permission", so the record cites the published version (Philosophical Books 51(4), 195–211) and treats the draft only as the copy read. Worth reading as a secondary report of Fricker's Epistemic Injustice ([LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md), unread), with page references to the book for its definitions and central cases, and as an argument that testimonial injustice needs a hearer's obligation to the speaker and can occur without individual identity prejudice. |
| [LIT-1867](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1867.md) | Source Incompatibilism and Its Alternatives | Timpe (2007), American Philosophical Quarterly 44(2), 143–155. The received taxonomy splits incompatibilists into leeway (alternative possibilities matter most) and source (ultimacy matters most). No leeway incompatibilist can rest on mere alternatives, which raise the luck objection, so every acceptable incompatibilism appeals to ultimacy. And ultimacy requires that the agent not be causally determined by anything outside her, which entails more than one open future and so some alternative possibility, however weak. So the best source incompatibilism is "wide", holding a weak alternative-possibilities condition entailed by ultimacy, and the taxonomy should be rejected. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1459](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1459.md)) in full, from the author's upload of the published pages (https://kevin-timpe.publicplatform.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/26/2018/12/source.pdf), an author's upload under [ADR-064](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-064.md). Worth reading as the argument that the best source incompatibilism is "wide": ultimacy requires indeterminism, indeterminism leaves some alternative, so an alternative-possibilities condition is entailed by the ultimacy condition, and the dichotomy between leeway and source incompatibilism should be dropped. Read it knowing that the entailed alternatives may be non-robust and do no explanatory work, and that it quotes Pereboom's book ([LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md), unread) at three places only. |
| [LIT-1868](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1868.md) | The Frankfurt Cases: The Moral of the Stories | Fischer (2010), Philosophical Review 119(3). The moral of the Frankfurt cases is that if causal determinism rules out moral responsibility, it is not in virtue of eliminating alternative possibilities. Against the Dilemma Defense: on the indeterministic horn, buffer cases (Hunt, Pereboom) remove every robust alternative; on the deterministic horn, assume determinism without assuming it removes alternatives, and determinism plus Black's counterfactual device together remove them, so Black does not "drop out", and the argument runs unchanged even granting that determinism removes alternatives. Widerker's requirement that the case satisfy IRR is rejected. Fischer allows that determinism may still undermine responsibility by another route, such as sourcehood. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1457](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1457.md)) in full, from the published PDF on andrewmbailey.com (https://andrewmbailey.com/jmf/Frankfurt_Cases_Moral_of_the_Stories.pdf), which the owner ruled a lawful copy on 2026-10-30. Worth reading as Fischer's reply to the Dilemma Defense: a deterministic Frankfurt case in which determinism and Black's device together, and neither alone, rule out alternatives, giving the conclusion that if determinism rules out responsibility it is not by eliminating alternative possibilities. Read it knowing that Fischer concedes causal determination may still matter, for instance by removing "sourcehood", and that Pereboom's buffer cases and Widerker's dilemma are reported, not argued in full. |
| [LIT-1869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1869.md) | Nature’s Queer Performativity | Barad (2012), Kvinder, Køn & Forskning 1–2:25–53, the authorized version of an essay first printed in Qui Parle (2011). It argues that identity, causality, space and time are performed, not given, in nature as well as culture. Lightning, stingray receptor cells, the dinoflagellate Pfiesteria and atoms are offered as "queer critters" whose behaviour a classical ontology of separate, determinate things cannot account for. Her agential realism replaces things with phenomena: an intra-action enacts an agential cut, "a 'local' resolution within the phenomenon of the inherent ontological indeterminacy", which yields agential separability, not absolute separation. The ethical upshot: there are no acts "against nature", only acts of nature, and accountability is for the cuts that are made. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1458.md)), from the journal's own PDF of the article (CC BY-NC) on tidsskrift.dk (tidsskrift.dk/KKF/article/download/28067/24695/65067), text extracted with pdftotext. This is the version Barad calls authorized; an earlier Qui Parle printing (2011) is, by her note 15, not the version she submitted. Worth reading as the record's first text of Barad's own: it states the agential cut in her words, as a local resolution, enacted by an intra-action within a phenomenon, of an inherent ontological indeterminacy, against the Cartesian cut as an inherent distinction. It is an essay, not an argument from data: its physics is the Bohr model and the which-path and quantum-eraser experiments as she reads them, and its other cases come from Kirby and Schrader. |
| [LIT-1874](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1874.md) v2 | Corporate Agency and Possible Futures | Mulgan (2018), Journal of Business Ethics 154(4). Read in full. It asks for an account of corporate agency that is "temporally robust", helping people in credible broken or digital futures resist domination by corporate groups, and argues that only "moralised extreme collectivism" is: moral agency only for groups reliably disposed to respond to moral reasons, full personhood open to the sophisticated among them, and no moral standing for a group with no mechanism for moral reasons. It reports Velasquez's individualism second-hand: the frame, the bitten bullet on the responsibility gap, the slippery slope to personhood and the Searlean premise, not the argument. | Active — read 2026-11-22 in full ([NOTE-2306](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2306.md)), from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0), https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10551-018-3887-1.pdf, which answered this time. Worth reading for its taxonomy of corporate agency (individualism; minimal, moderate and extreme collectivism), its reliability-based moral condition and its account of psychopathic corporate groups. Read it knowing that its case is from predicted future belief, and that it reports Velasquez only second-hand, with a citation that does not check out. |
| [LIT-1904](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1904.md) | The Lesser Existences: Étienne Souriau, an Aesthetics for the Virtual | Lapoujade (2017; English 2021). As usually described, a reading of Étienne Souriau's philosophy of the plural modes of existence, centred on "lesser existences": beings whose existence is incomplete or precarious and must be made more real. Unread: registered from metadata. What it says here is as the parent paper reports it. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-31 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. OpenAlex reports it closed. The University of Minnesota Press's open Manifold editions (manifold.umn.edu, all 202 projects listed through its API) do not include it. JSTOR and Project MUSE serve it to subscribers. The Internet Archive holds no copy, and a web search found no open copy. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1943](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1943.md) | The Elephant and the Blind: The Experience of Pure Consciousness: Philosophy, Science, and 500+ Experiential Reports | Metzinger (2024), MIT Press, open access. More than 500 anonymised reports of "pure awareness" from an online survey of meditators (1,403 usable respondents from 57 countries, 92 questionnaire items, twelve factors), grouped by theme in 34 chapters with commentary. The book's thesis is that consciousness can occur without time, self-location, an egoic self-model or a first-person perspective. It models pure awareness as a highest-level but "nonegoic self-model" of the organism's own epistemic openness, its tonic alertness, and so treats a first-person perspective as content, not a condition, of consciousness. The evidence is retrospective report from a self-selected sample. The methods chapter concedes that such reports cannot show the state was selfless when it occurred, while the summary calls nonegoic consciousness "empirically established". | Active — skimmed 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1499](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1499.md)), from the publisher's open-access PDF: the introduction, the theoretical commentary of chapters 2, 4, 8, 25, 28 and 31, all of chapter 34 and the epilogue's ethics sections were read; the report chapters were sampled, not read through. Worth reading as the fullest statement of Metzinger's later account of consciousness without a self. It offers "pure awareness" as minimal phenomenal experience and models it as a highest-level but nonegoic model of the organism's own epistemic openness. Its evidence is retrospective, self-selected reports from meditators. The methods chapter concedes the limits of that evidence and the summary overstates what it shows. |
| [LIT-1947](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1947.md) v2 | Artificial Suffering: An Argument for a Global Moratorium on Synthetic Phenomenology | Metzinger (2021), Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness 8(1):43–66, CC BY 4.0. Read in full. It argues for a global moratorium, until 2050, on research that directly aims at or knowingly risks synthetic phenomenology, because the risk of an "explosion of negative phenomenology" is incalculable without a theory of consciousness or of suffering. Suffering needs four necessary conditions: consciousness, a phenomenal self-model, negative valence integrated into it, and phenomenal transparency. So a conscious system without a self-model could not suffer, which the paper offers as a route to ethics by design. Bears on [QUESTION-368](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-368.md). | Active — read 2026-11-22 in full ([NOTE-2312](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2312.md)), from the published PDF deposited on Zenodo (record 7034864), fetched through Zenodo's records API; open access under CC BY 4.0. Worth reading as the source of the moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 and of the four-condition analysis of suffering that grounds it in a self. Read it knowing that the conditions are stipulated from the author's self-model theory and that its precaution runs in one direction. |
| [LIT-2191](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2191.md) | Essai sur le don. Forme et raison de l'échange dans les sociétés archaïques | Mauss (1925). A comparative essay on exchange in Polynesia, Melanesia, the American Northwest coast and ancient laws, asking what force in a thing given makes its recipient return it. Exchange there takes the form of gifts voluntary in theory and obligatory in fact, between collectivities, under three obligations: to give, to receive and to return. In Maori law the thing carries the giver's hau, which seeks its origin through every holder; in the potlatch the return is due with interest, and failing it costs face, rank and in the limit freedom (debt slavery). The conclusion holds that the same morality survives: an unreturned gift still makes its acceptor inferior and charity wounds, social insurance is right as a return owed to the worker for labour given, and the individual must still be made to rely on himself. | Active — skimmed 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1658.md); introduction, chapter I, part of chapter II and the conclusion read in full) from the Classiques des sciences sociales digital edition, transcribed from PUF's Sociologie et anthropologie (1968); worth reading as the founding statement of the three obligations of the gift (to give, to receive, to return) and for its claim that a gift accepted without return subordinates the receiver, which Mauss carries into a defence of social insurance as a return owed to the worker. Comparative and interpretive, built on second-hand ethnography; the hau reading rests on one informant's text in a translation Mauss himself calls abridged; the conclusion is moral and political argument, not a finding. |

| [LIT-2355](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2355.md) v2 | Genital Modifications in Prepubescent Minors: When May Clinicians Ethically Proceed? | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity (2024), DOI-10.1080/15265161.2024.2353823. | [LIT-2444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2444.md) v3 | Constitutivism's plight: inescapability, normativity, and relativism | Leffler (2024), The Philosophical Quarterly, DOI-10.1093/pq/pqae123. Read. Tested against four necessary features of normative force (invariance under desire change, ought-implies-can, ought-implies-can-fail, criticizability), psychological, further-factor and standpoint inescapability fail, and Korsgaard's plight inescapability, reconstructed as an agent's being continuously positioned to exercise its agency fully absent external limits, passes, but makes force relative to each agent's constitution. Constitutivists must accept relativism or give up the plight explanation. It bears on [QUESTION-128](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-128.md) and [QUESTION-129](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-129.md) as [LEAD-158](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-158.md)'s adversarial test. | Active — read 2026-11-22 ([NOTE-2360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2360.md), Read, in full), from the version of record (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) as the author posts it on his own site, https://www.olofleffler.com/uploads/1/2/2/9/122997280/constitutivisms_plight.pdf. Worth reading as the adversarial test of any constitutive route to the force of norms: four necessary features of force, three inescapability proposals that fail them, and a reconstructed plight inescapability that passes them and entails relativism. Read it knowing the author calls it exploratory and defends none of the views as true. |
| [LIT-2449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2449.md) v2 | Informed Consent | Eyal (2011), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Read on 2026-11-12 in [NOTE-1800](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1800.md): A survey of informed consent in bioethics: why it is required, what it consists in, and its status. §2 canvasses seven candidate justifications — protection (welfare), autonomy, prevention of abusive conduct, trust (forward- and backward-looking), self-ownership, non-domination, and personal integrity — and argues each faces serious objections, with autonomy (dominant since the 1970s) treated at length and found hard to ground as a complete justification. §§3–5 analyze consent itself (behavioral vs psychological; presumed/hypothetical consent), the information requirement, and voluntariness (coercion, undue inducement, "no choice" situations). §8 distinguishes natural-right, legal, epistemic and trust-based accounts of the requirement's status. §9 relates medical consent to sexual, contractual and political consent. §10 argues for a resilient "core" (risky, value-laden, invasive, refused interventions) and a weaker, more overridable "rim". Its account is [THEORY-1649](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1649.md). Registered from the exchange "Medical Ethics and Media Enshitification" (2026-11-11), where A cited it at A3 §3. | Active |

| [LIT-2493](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2493.md) v2 | Hermeneutical Injustice: Distortion and Conceptual Aptness | Falbo (2022), Hermeneutical Injustice: Distortion and Conceptual Aptness. Falbo argues that the dominant, "lacuna-centered" account of hermeneutical injustice (Fricker, and Pohlhaus, Dotson and Anderson who keep the lacuna requirement) is incomplete. Hermeneutical resources are not only interpretive (making experience intelligible) but productive: they organize people into roles and set "normative yardsticks" (Collins's controlling images, Tirrell on epithets, Jenkins on ontic injustice). So a concept can be available and understood yet fail to be applied where it fits, because distorting concepts "crowd out, defeat, or preempt" it. Her case is the Brock Turner trial: "rapist" was in the repertoire, but the "golden boy" image clashed with it. Read for the exchange "luria experiment design". | Active — Read on 2026-11-12 ([NOTE-1813](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1813.md)) from https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/648E80BC561C35DA399AA88BFB222C39/S0887536722000046a.pdf/div-class-title-hermeneutical-injustice-distortion-and-conceptual-aptness-div.pdf. |

| [LIT-2658](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2658.md) | Attributability, Answerability, and Accountability: In Defense of a Unified Account | Smith (2012). Attributability, Answerability, and Accountability: In Defense of a Unified Account. Ethics 122(3): 575-589. A reply to Shoemaker's (2011) three conceptions of responsibility. Smith argues that answerability, being open to a demand to justify one's attitudes and conduct, is the only kind of moral responsibility. What Shoemaker calls attributability is not responsibility at all, since we withhold aretaic labels from agents who are not answerable (the OCD case). What he calls accountability is answerability where a specific obligation to others has been violated. The different responses warranted differ by the seriousness of the failure, the relationship and the blamer's standing, which belong to the ethics of blame, not to the conditions of responsibility. Filed as a neighbour for Watson's "Two Faces of Responsibility", whose distinction it disputes. | Active — read in full 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2008](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2008.md)) from a copy of the published article on an MIT moral-psychology reading-group page (https://www.mit.edu/~shaslang/mprg/ASmithAAA.pdf). Filed as a neighbour for Watson, "Two Faces of Responsibility" ([LIT-2718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2718.md), Unavailable): the leading argument that the attributability/ accountability split Watson introduced does not mark distinct kinds of responsibility. | [LIT-2662](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2662.md) v2 | Moral Luck | Nagel (1979). Moral Luck. Mortal Questions, ch. 3. A revised version of his 1976 reply to Williams. Ordinary excuses rest on a condition that we are assessable only for what we control. Applied consistently, it erodes nearly all moral judgment, because what we are judged for depends on four kinds of luck: resultant (how things turn out), constitutive (the kind of person one is), circumstantial (the situations one faces) and causal (how one is determined by antecedent circumstances). Nagel holds that this is a genuine paradox, like scepticism, and not an error repaired by a refined condition. He rejects both paring action down to the will and the compatibilist reply, and traces the problem to the clash between the internal view of agency and the external view of acts as events. "In a sense", it has no solution. | Active — Read in full 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2015.md)) from an anthology reprint of the Mortal Questions text, posted as a course file on the University of Athens e-class site (course PHILOSOPHY921). Worth reading: the canonical statement of the problem of moral luck and its four kinds, and the source of the record's terms for them. |
| [LIT-2664](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2664.md) v3 | Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018 | National Transportation Safety Board (2019). Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (PB2019-101402). The NTSB found the probable cause to be the operator's failure to monitor the road and the automated system, through distraction by her phone. Uber ATG's inadequate risk assessment, operator oversight and countermeasures to automation complacency, "all a consequence of its inadequate safety culture", contributed, as did the impaired pedestrian's crossing and Arizona's oversight. The system was designed to rely on the operator to avoid collisions, and ATG's culture contributed to the operator's distraction itself. The report disclaims fault and blame. Elish names the moral crumple zone: when control over an automated system is distributed, responsibility for its failure can be misattributed to the nearest human operator, who had limited control, so that the operator absorbs moral and legal blame and "the integrity of the technological system" is protected. She argues it from the reception of Three Mile Island and Air France 447, through media framing, certification and the operator's legal final authority, and expects it of self-driving cars. | [LIT-2673](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2673.md) v2 | Coercion | Anderson (2006, rev. 2023). Coercion. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey of coercion as a technique of coercers and a reason for coercees. Its §3.2 finds no general theory of how coercion affects the coerced party's responsibility. The effect varies with the act and its moral context and runs mostly through justification, with excuse reserved mainly for a will that breaks down. Moral tests (Wertheimer, Pallikkathayil, lesser evil) and psychological ones (Feinberg) each cover only part of the field. Because coercion is strategic, the responsibility rule shapes coercers' incentives. It reports Galoob and Sheley's defence for a target whose decisional authority a coercive controller has usurped, and White's view that a conditional threat makes the coercee responsible for preventing what the coercer threatens. Bears on [CLAIM-708](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-708.md), [CLAIM-709](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-709.md) and [CASE-279](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-279.md). The Paradox of Algorithms and Blame on Public Decision-makers. Business and Politics 26(2): 200–217. DOI 10.1017/bap.2023.35. Two pre-registered vignette experiments on three representative US samples test whether algorithms shield public decision-makers from blame. A judge whose probation decision ends in a death is blamed no less for following an algorithm and not uniquely more for rejecting it; advice of any kind slightly raises blame, the algorithm is blamed without lowering the judge's share, and the rise for following it is mostly mediated by perceived abdication. Effects are small and fade in the third sample. Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account. Frontiers in Robotics and AI 5: 15. DOI 10.3389/frobt.2018.00015. Grounds the autonomous-weapons principle of meaningful human control in Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control: a system is under such control only if it tracks the relevant moral reasons of the humans who design and deploy it, and the relevant facts, and its behaviour traces to at least one human who understands its capabilities and that its effects will be attributed to them. Four years of fieldwork with ride-hail drivers (participant observation, 136 interviews with 63 drivers) find that, without managers or coworkers, drivers make their work meaningful through two workplace games: a relational game scored by the app's customer ratings, in which the platform appears as a facilitator and drivers follow its suggestions, and an efficiency game tracked with their own tools and sometimes by manipulating the algorithm, in which it appears as an opponent. | [LIT-2720](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2720.md) | Blame | Tognazzini and Coates (2014, rev. 2024). Blame. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey organised by two questions: which reactions constitute blame, and when blaming is appropriate. Accounts of what blame is are sorted into cognitive (Smart, Watson's aretaic blame, Hieronymi), emotional (Strawson, Wallace), conative (Sher, and Scanlon's modification of a relationship impaired by the wrong) and functional (protest, communication). Each is reported with its main objections: Wallace's charge that Scanlon "leaves the blame out of blame", and the problem of blaming strangers. Appropriateness depends on facts about the person blamed (agency, freedom, including coercion and manipulation), about the blaming interaction (proportionality, evidence) and about the blamer (standing: hypocrisy, complicity, meddling, moral luck, and Carbonell's claimant injustice). Read as the stand-in for Scanlon's Moral Dimensions and beside [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md) for Strawson. | Active — read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-1998](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1998.md)) from the plato.stanford.edu HTML, substantive revision of 30 Aug 2024; filed and read as the stand-in for Scanlon, Moral Dimensions ([LIT-2694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2694.md), Unavailable), and as a second neighbour, beside [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md), for Strawson, "Freedom and Resentment" ([LIT-2679](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2679.md), Unfetched). | [LIT-2724](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2724.md) v2 | Dirty Hands Defended | Linda Eggert (2023; issue 2025). Dirty Hands Defended. *Journal of Moral Philosophy* 22: 1–20. A dirty-hands case is a conflict between two actual duties: an act that is all things considered permissible, even required, can remain wrong, because the overridden duty survives as a pro tanto wrong or moral remainder that makes remorse apt and can ground duties of apology or compensation. Berlin's pluralism, "political consequentialism" and specificationism dissolve the problem at too high a price. Conflicts come from the world, "including other people's actions"; whether dirty hands are always produced by others' wrongdoing is left "for another day". Read in [NOTE-2040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2040.md); [THEORY-1982](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1982.md). | Active — read in full 2026-11-17 ([NOTE-2040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2040.md)) from the published version on the Oxford University Research Archive; worth reading here for its defence of the moral remainder in dirty-hands cases. | [LIT-2744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2744.md) v2 | Property and Ownership | Waldron & Penner, SEP "Property and Ownership" (2004; substantive revision 21 January 2026), skimmed in [NOTE-2050](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2050.md). Common, collective and private property differ in who decides; private property assigns resources "to the decisional authority of particular individuals", who decide "whether or not others are affected", so it "is continually in need of public justification". Analysis divides between the bundle of rights, property as a relation to a thing, and the owner's agenda-setting; default title is one liberty, one claim-right and two powers. Corporations have what blameworthy action needs but lack what angry blame needs. Shoemaker dissolves the paradox with his tripartite theory: attributability tracks quality of character, answerability quality of judgment (being "able in principle to answer the question, “Why did you do that?”"), and accountability quality of regard, grounded in the capacities for emotion and empathy and answered by gratitude and anger. Nyce (2013), "Just culture: "Evidence", power and algorithms", Journal of Hospital Administration 2(3): 73–77, read in [NOTE-2080](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2080.md). Algorithms that sort error into human error, at-risk and reckless behaviour treat culpability as an objective fact, but whether a response is just "depends on where one is located in the organization and medical competence hierarchy, and who gets to say"; a survey they relay found accountability rated worst and the most powerful group most satisfied. Just culture "risks becoming one more rhetoric or metric by which dominant groups can judge others". Worth reading here as an argued critique of just culture in practice: a response to error that one group finds just, others find unjust, and the difference tracks power, so a no-blame or just-culture scheme can carry blame along the hierarchy. A short essay; its empirical part is a survey it relays, not one it ran. |
